entry.title: This Completely Changes the Way We Build Production AI Agents (Vercel Eve)

media:group.media:title: This Completely Changes the Way We Build Production AI Agents (Vercel Eve)
media:group.media:description:
Vercel just open sourced their new AI agent framework Eve, and now your entire production AI agent can be just a single folder of mostly markdown. Instructions are markdown, tools are TypeScript, skills and subagents are just nested folders. Eve compiles the whole thing into a durable service you deploy with one command. Durable execution, an isolated sandbox, human approvals, and evals all ship in the box.
In this video I show you how Eve works and a data analyst agent I built with Eve without writing the code or running a single command myself. I just prompt Claude Code with Vercel's plugin, and it scaffolds the agent, runs it, and deploys it. It could not be easier now to build production ready AI agents! This video is a partnership with Vercel, and every opinion in it is my own.

entry.title: Pydantic AI 2.0: The New Best Way to Build AI Agents is Composing Capabilities

media:group.media:title: Pydantic AI 2.0: The New Best Way to Build AI Agents is Composing Capabilities
media:group.media:description:
The new best way to build AI agents is to compose capabilities, instead of every agent being a unorganized pile of tools, instructions, and guardrails. That is the shift in Pydantic AI 2.0, and it changes how you build every agent.
A capability is a self-contained brick that bundles its own instructions, tools, model settings, and hooks. You compose an agent by snapping bricks together, and the same brick drops into any other agent unchanged.
In this video I showcase a real support agent built entirely out of capabilities, then reuse one of them in a completely different agent without changing a line. Building production ready AI agents has never been easier!

entry.title: I Love the Karpathy LLM Wiki but it Doesn't Scale. Here's What Does.

media:group.media:title: I Love the Karpathy LLM Wiki but it Doesn't Scale. Here's What Does.
media:group.media:description:
Markdown makes great memory for an AI agent - a Karpathy-style LLM wiki, an Obsidian second brain it reads and writes. If the agent is just yours, a folder of markdown is hard to beat: simple, yours, all in git. My second brain is exactly that!
It falls apart the second you ship that agent to other people. Now the memory has many users at once, the data behind it changes in real time, and you need retrieval and access control a pile of files can't give you. That's not a memory problem anymore - you need a context layer.
So I take an agent and build it that layer with Redis, going deep on two new pieces of Redis Iris: Context Retriever, which turns your data into tools the agent can safely call, and Agent Memory, which scales recall across thousands of conversations.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Thanks to Redis for working with me on this video! I've been looking for a while for the best database platform to make exactly this video.
I focus on the two newest pieces, Context Retriever and Agent Memory. Iris is actually five tools, those two plus Redis Data Integration, LangCache, and Redis Search. All seriously worth a look: https://fandf.co/439eNyo

entry.title: Finally, an Open Standard for the Karpathy LLM Wiki is HERE

media:group.media:title: Finally, an Open Standard for the Karpathy LLM Wiki is HERE
media:group.media:description:
Google just quietly shipped the Open Knowledge Format (OKF): an open standard that formalizes Andrej Karpathy's LLM wiki pattern into plain markdown any AI can read with zero integration. No plugin, RAG pipeline, or vector DB. You point your agent at a folder and ask it anything as long as it knows OKF!
You probably already have a personal agent and search that works well. And you're probably building some version of a "second brain." So why is it still basically impossible to hand your knowledge to someone else's AI and have it just work? The answer is we never agreed on a format - and that's exactly what Google has now solved.
In this video I break down OKF, talk about why it's so important, and even give you a bundle so you agent can immediately search through my YouTube content.

entry.title: My AI Memory Now Follows Me Across Every Tool!

media:group.media:title: My AI Memory Now Follows Me Across Every Tool!
media:group.media:description:
Your AI agent's memory is trapped inside one tool. The second you switch from Claude Code to Codex or Pi, all that context is gone - and recently I've been switching constantly!
So I started using Walrus Memory: a memory layer that lives outside any single agent, encrypted and owned by you. As I'm working with my agents like my second brain, it pulls out the important details and saves them as memories, and a brand-new agent from a different provider recalls them instantly. Claude wrote the memory, Pi read it, and neither one knew about the other.
Setup is a single prompt! The memories are tied to a key you own, encrypted before they're ever stored, and you decide which agent can read what (and revoke it any time). It's AI memory you actually own.
Try it free: http://bit.ly/43oODrJ
Thanks to Walrus for working with me on this!

entry.title: The Creators of Claude Code and OpenClaw don't Prompt Their Agents Anymore?!

media:group.media:title: The Creators of Claude Code and OpenClaw don't Prompt Their Agents Anymore?!
media:group.media:description:
The best AI engineers barely prompt their agents anymore. Sounds crazy I know! They build a loop that does the prompting for them and let it run for hours while they step away. The head of Claude Code at Anthropic put it bluntly: he doesn't prompt Claude, he has loops running that prompt Claude for him.
The only problem is this gets expensive (and hallucinations compound) - you need a harness with observability that can run reliably not always using the expensive frontier models.
So I built one! It's a TypeScript app that runs Pi (on Kimi) in a loop, stores every run in a database, and shows it all in a dashboard. And the loop isn't one agent on repeat, it's agents prompting agents: an orchestrator decides the next tasks and spins up workers to run them in parallel. Think of it like an advanced Ralph loop with more control!

entry.title: Omnigent: The New Meta-Harness for EVERY Coding Agent - Claude Code, Codex, Pi, More

media:group.media:title: Omnigent: The New Meta-Harness for EVERY Coding Agent - Claude Code, Codex, Pi, More
media:group.media:description:
The way the best engineers use AI is shifting fast. Instead of committing to a single provider, they use the right model for each job - like using Claude for implementation, and Codex for reviewing, and Kimi/Minimax for simple tasks. The piece we have been missing is a clean way to orchestrate all of those models together. That is exactly what Omnigent is: a meta-harness that runs Claude Code, Codex, and Pi as interchangeable workers under one roof!
In this video I show you how to get it running and put it to work live. One AI agent plans a coding task, hands the implementation to Claude Code in its own git worktree, then routes the finished diff to a different provider, Codex, for review. You also get a governance layer for human in the loop, and sessions that follow you from terminal to browser to phone. And since I build my own agent engine, Archon, every day, I will give you a straight take on where a meta-harness fits.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
